The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Its original purpose was to record the names of those entitled to receive shares of the conquest booty and charitable funds, and to classify them according to the kind and rank of their entitlement.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The order of distribution was as follows: first the Prophet’s wives; then the Prophet’s Companions, beginning with the early emigrants; then the Anṣār; and finally the tribes that had taken part in the conquests and were living in the conquered regions.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

This system clearly created differences in rank. Even so, the establishment of the dīwān was an important step in the development of organized government. It contained some of the first features of an emerging state.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This, more specifically, is what historians refer to as the “System of ʿUmar.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But there were also negative features in the conquest system we have described—or, more precisely, in the way that system worked in practice.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One of them was the isolation we mentioned earlier.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The Arab conquerors remained separate from the process of social production and from social life more generally. Their activity stayed concentrated within the military settlements. This also reflected a sense that they stood above the local population, while their own society remained divided internally along tribal lines.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The class differences that also existed among them were another matter. These were a natural result of the stage of social development through which Arab society was then passing, as it took its first steps toward a more developed class society.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar’s role in this transition helped prepare the way for the establishment of the state as an organized political system.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

He did not allow the conquering armies simply to act as they wished. Alongside his strict instructions that they follow the rules already mentioned, and his repeated orders that the inhabitants of conquered lands be treated with tolerance, he also kept close control over the soldiers themselves.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

He counted them, recorded their ranks and tribal affiliations, and entered all of this carefully in the records of the dīwān. Under him, the dīwān became an organized administrative institution, which the Umayyad caliphs later developed further.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
His aim was to ensure that the booty from the conquests was distributed according to a fixed system rather than according to the wishes of military commanders.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
ʿUmar also closely watched the conduct of the governors he appointed over the conquered lands and regularly demanded detailed reports about their behavior.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
If he learned that one of these governors had wronged the local population or deprived someone of a rightful claim, he punished the governor firmly and severely.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These measures, instructions, and legal judgments became known collectively as the “System of ʿUmar.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The term may also include the policy he followed toward Arab Christians living in Syria, Palestine, and Iraq.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
First, he ordered that especially heavy taxes be imposed on them in order to encourage them to enter Islam. His explanation is striking: these people were Arabs, and the Arabs were the army of Islam.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Second, even if these Arab Christians did not convert, he allowed them to serve in the conquering Arab army with the same rights as Muslim Arabs. This privilege was not extended to non-Muslims from the non-Arab populations of the conquered lands.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Can we conclude from these two policies toward Arab Christians that ʿUmar was trying to build an Arab solidarity rather than an Islamic solidarity that went beyond the Arabs?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
I am inclined to answer yes—though not without qualification.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
D — The Process of Social and Cultural Interaction
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
There can be no serious dispute that social and cultural interaction took place between the Arabs and the peoples of the conquered lands.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Nor can there be any serious dispute about the major role this interaction played in the development of Arab thought and Arab society.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We will return to this subject many times. For now, however, our question is more specific: When did this interaction begin, and how did it begin?
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The complicated conditions of the conquests delayed the process.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arab communities in the conquered lands were occupied with military life and with the organization of military, administrative, and tax systems.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As we saw earlier, these conditions led the conquerors to live apart from the local population. Above all, they remained separate from the process of material production.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Their daily lives were centered in the military settlements built for the conquering armies and for migrants who had come from the Arabian Peninsula with them.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It would therefore be fair to describe the Arab communities of this period mainly as military communities.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Even the institutions of government, administration, and finance had this divided character.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Their connection with the everyday lives of the local population was weak. They functioned as institutions “above” society, operating on its surface and dealing with the outward affairs of life without yet reaching deeply into its internal structure.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
For this reason, we can say that the conditions needed for real social and cultural interaction had not yet developed during the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That is why we find little evidence of such interaction that is especially striking.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

But the situation changed once the Arabs began to settle permanently, once their communities put down deeper roots in the lands where they lived, once the state and its institutions developed at both higher and lower levels, once Arabs entered the process of material production, and once their ownership of land and other property became firmly established.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As soon as these conditions came together, the effects of social and cultural interaction became clear.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That interaction then began to play the historical role we mentioned earlier and will examine more closely later.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

This realistic and historical way of looking at the question also helps us understand a claim made by some modern researchers: that the Arabs rejected the cultures of the peoples who became part of their vast state.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
What actually happened was not rejection.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It was a delay in the process of social and cultural interaction.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
That delay was an objective historical fact with objective causes, some of which we have already described.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Rejection, by contrast, would have been a deliberate act of choice.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But historical processes cannot be explained simply by personal or collective acts of will.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
For this reason, the following explanation cannot adequately account for what happened:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

“During ʿUmar’s reign, the Arabs succeeded in bringing together fragments of many different kingdoms whose peoples possessed very different cultures: Egypt, including Alexandria, then a center of learning; Persia and Iraq, which were full of different religious and philosophical movements such as Nestorianism, Mazdakism, and Manichaeism; and Syria, where the Jacobites lived alongside followers of other ancient religions. (...) The Arabs therefore found themselves surrounded by a flood of knowledge from which they could have drawn if they had wished. But at first, influenced by pride in their religion and unwilling to become pupils of people who had now become their subjects, the Muslims rejected these cultures and turned away from them except in a few rare cases. They did not begin learning from their people until the circumstances of life brought them down from their position of supremacy.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This kind of explanation of social and historical developments lacks a scientific method.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Social and cultural interaction between peoples is a large and complicated historical process. It depends on objective conditions, and those conditions are themselves complex.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Arabs at the beginning of the conquests were in precisely such a situation.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As we have just seen, their relationship with the peoples of the conquered lands did not yet place them in the kind of social setting where cultural and social interaction could fully develop.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
During the first stage, the Arabs had kept themselves apart from the main areas of social activity in those countries.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In other words, they had not yet entered the field in which interaction naturally develops through objective historical processes.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
It is therefore not correct to say that the Arabs rejected the cultures of these peoples.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
And even if such a rejection had taken place, it would not have been enough to prevent the interaction from eventually happening.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
There is another problem with the claim that the Arabs did not begin to learn from these cultures “until the circumstances of life brought them down from their position of supremacy.”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We do not know exactly when this researcher believes the Arabs lost that position.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

Perhaps he means the period when Persians or Turks became prominent in the government of the Abbasid state, since it seems unlikely that he means the final collapse of Arab political rule in the thirteenth century.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
If he does mean the Abbasid period—and even that would require discussion—then he has simply left the Umayyad period out of his account.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Yet already under the Umayyads, during a period of fully Arab political rule, Arab society showed unmistakable signs of influence from the cultures and institutions of the conquered peoples.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We can see this in the philosophical ideas and logical methods that appeared among various religious and political groups, especially the Muʿtazilites.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We can also see it in the administrative, financial, political, and other institutions of the Umayyad state.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
These are clear examples of cultural influence. There is nothing here that can reasonably be described as the rejection claimed by that researcher.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
2 — Islamic Law During the Period of Conquest
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Even during the early period when the Arabs still lived in relative isolation, the conquests opened new possibilities for the development of Islamic law.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They created wider scope for the use of reason and personal judgment—what Islamic legal thought calls ijtihād.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

What matters here is that the new conditions created by the conquests produced a broad range of new needs and problems. This gave a powerful new impulse to the development of Islamic law through rational judgment—in other words, through ijtihād based on reasoned opinion.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
As we saw in Chapter Two, ijtihād had already been used before the conquests.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But it had operated within a fairly narrow range because life in the Arabian Peninsula itself had been relatively limited in scope.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We can also put the matter another way.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The general legal principles found in the two main sources of Islamic law—the Qurʾān and the Sunna—often first appeared in connection with a particular event or case. From that particular case, the principle would then be extended and turned into a general rule.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In this sense, we can say that almost all of these general rules developed out of specific and recurring situations in Arab life within the peninsula.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Because the range of those situations was still relatively limited, it was often easy to apply an existing text to a new case by analogy.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
But Arab life expanded as the Islamic movement developed.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Social relations also began to change.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Islamic law therefore had to respond to new needs and problems created by this development and apply its general principles in new ways.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
This required more active use of reason.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

The effort to apply Islamic law to new events and new problems therefore gave thought more room to move. It encouraged people to judge situations in ways that increasingly showed the influence of rational reflection.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In these completely new conditions, the caliphs and Companions faced situations unlike anything they had dealt with before.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
They therefore had to think more deeply about both general and specific laws before applying them to these unfamiliar circumstances.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
Among the Rightly Guided Caliphs, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was the boldest in using ijtihād based on personal judgment to deal with these new situations.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We have already seen him do this in many areas.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
He set aside one rule that had existed during the Prophet’s lifetime, modified another, and approached still others in new ways.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
In each case, he used a flexible understanding of the relationship between law and changing circumstances.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
One example was his decision to end the share of charitable funds given to the muʾallafa qulūbuhum—those whose hearts were to be won over.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

During the Prophet’s lifetime, such people had been given money from charitable funds in order to attract them to Islam. This might be because their faith was weak, because their hostility needed to be prevented, or because they held an important position among their people.
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
The practice was based on the Qurʾānic verse:
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
“Charitable funds are only for the poor, the needy, those employed to collect them, and those whose hearts are to be won over...”
The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
